questions.stem: A 36-year-old man presented unwell with a 2-week history of fever and new-onset intense myalgia. He also initially had abdominal pain, diarrhea, and vomiting. He was usually well and did not take any regular medications. He was a nonsmoker and did not take any recreational drugs. He had arrived in the United States 3 weeks earlier from rural Mexico. For his farewell party his friends in Mexico prepared for him smoked boar meat. On examination, his temperature was 38.5°C, his heart rate was 110 beats/minute, his respiratory rate was 26 breaths/minute, and his oxygen saturations were 93% on room air. He had periorbital edema and conjunctivitis, respiratory distress with bibasal crackles, and peripheral edema. Investigations: CPK 512 U/L EKG: flat T waves in I, AVL, V5, and V6 Cardiac MR: gadolinium enhancement in the lateral and inferolateral epicardial areas
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Trichinellosis This patient most likely has trichinellosis with myocarditis as a disease manifestation. He likely acquired Trichinella spiralis from consumption of undercooked boar meat. Clinically relevant clues to the diagnosis include the ingestion of undercooked boar, the GI syndrome followed by intense myalgia and fever, as well as periorbital edema and conjunctivitis. Although enteroviral and influenza myocarditis can present with a viral prodrome and malaise, the myalgias would be milder, and there would not be associated facial edema. Although the ECG findings and elevated enzymes would fit a diagnosis of lateral wall MI, the additional symptoms and findings would not be explained by this diagnosis. While Brucella is present in wild boar meat, most infections are due to skinning and meat handling, and the symptoms of myocarditis do not fit the clinical presentations of brucellosis.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q16

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man presented with a 24-hour history of an excruciating headache, photophobia, and neck stiffness. The headache had been gradual in onset, progressing in severity. Seven days earlier he had returned from a 2-month holiday in Vietnam where he had been staying with family. He had a history of hypertension and osteoarthritis of his knees and took regular amlodipine. Investigations: Peripheral white blood cell count 7.3 ×109/L Peripheral eosinophil count 1.5 ×109/L CSF white cell count 346 ×106/L; 30% eosinophils CSF red cell count 22 ×106/L CSF protein 560 mg/L CSF/plasma glucose 3.5/4.8 mmol/L CSF microscopy: no organisms seen CT head with contrast – mild leptomeningeal enhancement
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely source of the infecting organism?
questions.explanation: Consumption of undercooked snails The infective organism is most likely to be Angiostrongylus cantonensis, the rat lungworm. This is due to the geographical exposure (SE Asia), the incubation period (average 10 days), the clinical features (excruciating progressive headache), and the eosinophilic meningitis without raised red cells. The commonest source of A. cantonensis is consumption of raw or undercooked snails.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q12

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman presented with high fevers, severe muscle pain, tenderness, and swelling. There was no significant past medical history. There were no other symptoms reported, no recent unusual activities, although she did recall eating some undercooked pork 3 weeks previously. On examination her temperature was 38.6 oC. She was tender and had limited movement due to pain in the muscles of her shoulder girdle, upper arms, and forearms. There were numerous subungual splinter hemorrhages seen, and she had bilateral conjunctival hemorrhages. Mild hepatomegaly was palpable. Investigations: Total white cell count 13.2 ×109/L Eosinophil count 4.1 ×109/L
questions.lead_in: What parasite is most likely to be responsible?
questions.explanation: Trichinella spiralis The most likely diagnosis is infection with Trichinella spiralis, a tissue nematode. It is transmitted through ingestion of raw or undercooked contaminated meat (encysted larvae). Muscle stage develops when intestinal adult-derived larvae disseminate hematogenously (or via lymphatics) and invade striated muscle.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q19

questions.stem: A 46-year-old Thai woman presented with a sudden onset headache and right-sided weakness. Her temperature was 36.5°C, blood pressure 124/74 mmHg, and heart rate 88 beats/ minute. Her Glasgow Coma Score was 14/15. She was drowsy but rousable. She had a right-sided flaccid hemiparesis. An urgent CT scan of her head was arranged. Investigations: Eosinophils 5.9 ×109/L CT scan of head: On further questioning her partner revealed that she had also had a prolonged history of recurrent superficial swellings on her arms and torso. These would last for 1–2 weeks, resolve then recur weeks to months later. She had been born and brought up in a small village in northern Thailand, but had emigrated 6 years previously. She had spent 3 months of each year since then in Thailand.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely source of her infection?
questions.explanation: Uncooked freshwater fish This is a clinical case of gnathostomiasis, evidenced by the recurrent cutaneous swellings, the epidemiologic risk factors associated with Thailand, and the investigative findings. Gnathostoma spinigerum is acquired by eating undercooked infected poultry, snake, or freshwater fish, or by drinking water contaminated with infected Cyclops crustaceans. (Image from Assessments. In Cohen J, Powderly W , Opal S, eds. Infectious Diseases. 4th ed. Elsevier; 2017.)
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 9 Q42

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman presented with migratory swellings over her right arm and back. They typically lasted for 1–3 days and were hot, red, painful, and itchy. She had returned 4 weeks earlier from a 12-month job in Cameroon. A presumptive diagnosis of loiasis was made, pending investigations.
questions.lead_in: What was the most likely vector for her infection?
questions.explanation: Chrysops deerfly This is the vector responsible for the transmission of Loa loa, with the female of the species biting during the day, especially in the wet season.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 9 Q50

questions.question: Patient traveled to India, presents scrotal edema with inflammation of the lymphatic path of a lower limb.

parts.text: What is the most likely organism
What is the mechanism for explaining edema
Name three diagnostic tests
He develops cellulitis of the lower limb, which organism is most likely involved?
Name 3 ways to prevent cellulitis in this patient

cohort_answer.text:
Most likely organism: Wuchereria bancrofti
Mechanism for edema: Redbook: Adult worms cause lymphatic dilatation and dysfunction, which result in abnormal lymph flow and eventually may lead to lymphedema in the legs, scrotal area (for W bancrofti only), and arms.
Three diagnostic tests: Circulating filarial antigen assay; Blood smears (10pm-4am); PCR; Serology; Ultrasound and lymphoscintigraphic techniques
Organism for cellulitis: Streptococcus pyogenes. Dx: Acute Dermato-Lymphangio-Adenitis (ADLA). Attacks of ADLA are characterised by localized pain and tenderness, lymphadenitis and/or lymphangitis and/or cellulitis and local warmth, with (mostly 97% cases) or without systemic manifestations of fever, nausea and vomiting. Secondary infections due to bacteria like Group A streptococcus are responsible.
Three ways to prevent cellulitis: Control of edema/promotion of lymph flow; Rigorous hygiene/foot care; Good glycaemic control if diabetic; Long term antibiotics ("In patients with advanced stages of lymphedema, proper local care of the limb is not always possible due to deep skin folds or warty projections. If such patients have recurrent (=>2 episodes) ADLA attacks, long-term antibiotic therapy using oral penicillin or long acting benzathine penicillin 1.2 MU, deep IM every 3 weeks is indicated")

questions.question: An Ethiopian man presents with dyspnea, wheezing and hemoptysis, and is diagnosed with asthma and treated with inhaled beclomethasone and oral prednisone for exacerbations. Despite this, he has hemoptysis four more times. His blood work shows eosinophils at 1.5 x 10^9/ml.

parts.text: What is the most likely diagnosis?
Name three tests that would help in diagnosis and which samples to send for each.
Which viral infection predisposes to severe infection?
Name two management recommendations.

questions.model_answer:
a) Most likely diagnosis: Strongyloides stercoralis hyperinfection syndrome, precipitated by the corticosteroid therapy given for presumed asthma.
b) Three helpful tests: (1) Multiple stool examinations (O&P x3, or agar plate culture) for larvae - stool. (2) Strongyloides serology (IgG ELISA) - serum. (3) Sputum or bronchoalveolar lavage microscopy for filariform larvae - respiratory sample.
c) HTLV-1 (human T-lymphotropic virus type 1) co-infection predisposes to severe/disseminated strongyloidiasis by promoting a Th1-skewed immune response that impairs the Th2-mediated eosinophilic defense against the parasite.
d) Two management recommendations: (1) Discontinue/taper corticosteroids and other immunosuppression as soon as possible. (2) Treat with ivermectin (daily until larvae clear from stool/sputum, continued at least 2 weeks after clearance), with adjunctive albendazole considered.
questions.beyond_mandell: Clinical presentation is classic for corticosteroid-precipitated Strongyloides hyperinfection; the chapter is filed under tissue nematodes/filariae, so this diagnosis is a plausible mismatch versus the labeled chapter topic.

questions.question: ADULT section. Name parasitic organism associated with the stem (genus and species).

parts.text: 50 year old from Taiwan with recurrent cholangitis and cholangiocarcinoma
37 year old from Tanzania with portal hypertension
36 year old from Ethiopia with interstitial keratitis poor vision
38 year old from Mozambique with fibrosis in the bladder

questions.model_answer:
a) 50-year-old from Taiwan with recurrent cholangitis and cholangiocarcinoma: Clonorchis sinensis.
b) 37-year-old from Tanzania with portal hypertension: Schistosoma mansoni (hepatosplenic schistosomiasis).
c) 36-year-old from Ethiopia with interstitial keratitis and poor vision: Onchocerca volvulus (river blindness).
d) 38-year-old from Mozambique with bladder wall fibrosis: Schistosoma haematobium.
questions.cites: Mandell pp. 3453-3461 (Schistosoma/Clonorchis); Onchocerca is outside this trematode chapter

questions.question: 34-M who presents with a single documented fever, peri-orbital edema and conjunctivitis with neck pain. One week ago, he had non-bloody diarrhea. He was recently out in his cabin where he ate wild fungi and smoked game meats.

parts.text: What is the clinical diagnosis
List 2 routine tests that you can do to support your diagnosis
Name one test you can do to confirm the diagnosis

questions.model_answer:
a) Clinical diagnosis: Trichinellosis (Trichinella spiralis infection), from ingestion of undercooked wild game meat - classic triad of fever, periorbital edema, and myositis (neck pain/myalgia), preceded by an enteric phase (diarrhea).
b) Two routine supportive tests: complete blood count showing eosinophilia, and creatine kinase (elevated from associated myositis).
c) Confirmatory test: Trichinella serology (ELISA for anti-Trichinella IgG) or muscle biopsy demonstrating encysted larvae.

questions.question: Patient from India with scrotal swelling

parts.text: What is the diagnosis and what is the organism?
What are 3 ways to diagnose?
The pt presents with worse edema and sounds like cellulitis. What is the Dx?
Provide 3 prevention strategies.

cohort_answer.text: Diagnosis/organism: Filariasis - Wuchereria bancrofti. Diagnosis methods: Serological-antigen detection; US findings; PCR. Worsening edema/cellulitis Dx: Streptococcal cellulitis. Prevention strategies: Beta-lactam prophylaxis; Pressure support; Elevate legs; Treat tinea infection.

questions.question: PM Q20. Indian male with swollen painful scrotum (chronic)

parts.text: a) What is likely cause?
b) What 3 tests can you do?
c) Several years later 'post Tx' develops acute swollen painful leg - what is most likely pathogen? What 3 methods could be used to prevent future episodes?

cohort_answer.text:
Wuchereria bancrofti, Brugia malayi and Brugia timori (Lymphatic Filariasis - W. bancrofti 90% of cases). Spread via mosquito (Anopheles-Africa, Culex-Americas, Aedes/Mansonia-Pacific/Asia). Adult worms live 5-7yrs, release millions of microfilariae into blood
Detection of circulating filarial antigen (W. bancrofti only) - ELISA; Blood smear (check between 10pm-2am for circulating microfilaria); Ultrasound/lymphoscintigraphic imaging (filarial dance sign); Serology; PCR/antifilarial antibody tests
Streptococcus skin infection most likely pathogen. Prevention: Compression stockings; Scrotal sling; Elevation/massage; Surgical intervention (complete decongestive therapy); Prophylactic antibiotics if >3 episodes/year

questions.question: Trivia: Seven tropical infections that can be diagnosed with peripheral blood smear (Giemsa)

parts.text: Name the seven infections

cohort_answer.text: African/American trypanosomiasis, Babesia, Bartonella (bacilliformis - Oroya fever), Filariasis, Malaria, TBRF (tick-borne relapsing fever), LBRF (louse-borne relapsing fever) (also Histoplasmosis, Leptospirosis mentioned)

questions.question: Name the most likely parasitic pathogen.

parts.text: Pt with portal hypertension
Pt with bladder fibrosis
Recurrent cholangitis and fibrosis
Sclerosing keratitis

cohort_answer.text: Portal hypertension: Schistosoma japonicum or mansoni. Bladder fibrosis: Schistosoma haematobium. Recurrent cholangitis and fibrosis: Clonorchis sinensis; Opisthorchis viverrini/felineus; Fasciola hepatica; Ascaris lumbricoides. Sclerosing keratitis: Acanthamoeba; Onchocerciasis.

questions.question: Man from India with groin swelling, leg swelling.

parts.text: What is the pathogen
What is mechanism of scrotal swelling?
List 3 investigations that would give you the diagnosis.

questions.model_answer:
a) Pathogen: Wuchereria bancrofti (lymphatic filariasis).
b) Mechanism of scrotal swelling: adult worms residing in the lymphatics cause chronic lymphangitis, lymphatic dilation, and lymphatic obstruction, leading to lymph stasis/lymphedema and hydrocele formation in the scrotal lymphatics.
c) Three investigations: (1) Nocturnal peripheral blood smear for microfilariae (timed to nocturnal periodicity). (2) Circulating filarial antigen test (immunochromatographic card test). (3) Scrotal ultrasound demonstrating motile adult worms within dilated lymphatics ("filarial dance sign").

questions.question: Name the parasite that is associated with various long term effects

parts.text: Cholangiocarcinoma and recurrent cholangitis from taiwan
Portal hypertension from ?subsaharan africa
Keratitis and blindness from Ethiopia
Bladder wall fibrosis ?subsaharan africa

questions.model_answer: Cholangiocarcinoma/recurrent cholangitis from Taiwan: Clonorchis sinensis. Portal hypertension from sub-Saharan Africa: Schistosoma mansoni. Keratitis and blindness from Ethiopia: Onchocerca volvulus. Bladder wall fibrosis from sub-Saharan Africa: Schistosoma haematobium.

questions.question: Guy lives in the wilderness, eats wild fungi and game meat. 2 weeks ago, had abdominal pain and diarrhea. Now has peri-orbital edema, neck pain especially the neck and conjunctival injections.

parts.text: What is the most likely pathogen
What are 2 abnormalities on ROUTINE bloodwork that is characteristics of this infection
How do you diagnosis the infection

cohort_answer.text: Pathogen: Trichinella spiralis. Bloodwork abnormalities: Eosinophilia/Leukocytosis; Elevated CK; Elevated LDH; Hypergammaglobulinemia. Diagnosis: Trichinella serology (ELISA), results can be confirmed with Western blot, not detected until >3 weeks; Muscle biopsy (definitive diagnosis)

parts.text: What is the most common tissue nematode (to species level) associated with lymphatic filariasis?

questions.model_answer: Wuchereria bancrofti is the most common tissue nematode causing lymphatic filariasis worldwide.

questions.question: A patient from Indonesia presents with fever, non-productive cough, and dyspnea. Chest x-ray demonstrates bilateral opacities. Laboratory investigations reveal elevated IgE and eosinophilia.

parts.text: What condition does he likely have?
List ONE test that should be performed to confirm the diagnosis.
List TWO other chronic conditions associated with this organism.

questions.model_answer:
a) Tropical pulmonary eosinophilia (TPE), a hypersensitivity manifestation of lymphatic filariasis (Wuchereria bancrofti or Brugia malayi).
b) Confirmatory test: antifilarial antibody serology (elevated antifilarial IgG titers), often paired with markedly elevated total IgE.
c) Two other chronic conditions associated with this organism: lymphedema/elephantiasis, and hydrocele.

questions.question: You are assessing a young man with fever, nuchal rigidity. LP is done and shows 88 WBCs (58% eosinophils, 28% neuts, 14% lymphs), glucose 2.5, and protein 0.5. He just returned from 2 weeks in Thailand where he tried many street foods, including one with snails that may have been undercooked.

parts.text: What is the MOST likely infecting organism (genus and species)?
What is the definitive host of this organism?
He has two intracranial lesions on MRI. What other pharmacologic treatment would assist with his management?

questions.model_answer:
a) Most likely organism: Angiostrongylus cantonensis (rat lungworm), causing eosinophilic meningitis after ingestion of undercooked snails.
b) Definitive host: the rat (Rattus species).
c) Corticosteroids (e.g., dexamethasone) should be added, as they reduce the inflammatory response to dying larvae and have been shown to hasten symptom resolution; anthelmintic therapy is generally avoided or used cautiously (with steroid cover) because killing larvae can worsen inflammation.

questions.question: Tropical disease question on filariasis

parts.text: What is the most common organism of lymphatic filariasis?
A patient just returned from India with wheezing, and dyspnea and found to have elevated peripheral eosinophilia. What is this complication associated with lymphatic filariasis?
What is one laboratory test that can confirm the diagnosis?
What are TWO long-term complications from the above condition?

questions.model_answer:
a) Wuchereria bancrofti is the most common cause of lymphatic filariasis.
b) This presentation (wheezing, dyspnea, marked peripheral eosinophilia) represents tropical pulmonary eosinophilia (TPE), a hyperresponsiveness syndrome to filarial antigens.
c) Confirmatory laboratory test: antifilarial antibody serology (elevated antifilarial IgG titers), often with markedly elevated total IgE.
d) Two long-term complications: progressive interstitial lung disease/pulmonary fibrosis if untreated, and bronchiectasis.

questions.question: Q79 (2012 AM). Strongyloides with filarial co-infection.

parts.text: A) What is the risk of ivermectin?
B) 2 ways to handle those from an endemic region for strongyloides going to start immunosuppression?

cohort_answer.text: A) Administration of ivermectin to highly loa loa microfilaremic subjects can precipitate life-threatening encephalopathy. Relative contraindications: confirmed/suspected loa loa infection (albendazole alternative), previous hypersensitivity, weight<15kg or age<1 year, pregnant women (category C). B) 'Test and treat' approach; empiric administration of ivermectin to at-risk patients before immunosuppression before results are back.

questions.question: Q51 (2006 PM). Somebody who has come back from west Africa with eosinophilia. What organisms that you would suspect if the patient has the following:

parts.text: Migratory swelling
Localized dermatitis
Wheeze/cough
Lymphedema

cohort_answer.text: Migratory swelling: Loa loa, Gnathostoma spinigerum (SE Asia only). Localized dermatitis: Schistosoma spp, Onchocerca volvulus. Wheeze/cough: Loffler's syndrome (Ascaris lumbricoides, Necator americanus/Ancylostoma duodenale, Strongyloides stercoralis, Toxocara canis, Paragonimus), tropical pulmonary eosinophilia (Wuchereria). Lymphedema: Wuchereria bancrofti/Brugia malayi.

questions.question: Q52 (2010 PM). Woman immigrated from India 6 years ago. Now has asymptomatic eosinophilia on 3 occasions for the past 3 months. IgE elevated. Normal LFTs, OB negative and stool O+P negative

parts.text: A) Name the top 3 diagnoses
B) List 3 investigations you would do next

cohort_answer.text: A) Strongyloides stercoralis; Schistosomiasis; HIV; Helminths (filariasis). B) HIV serology; Strongyloides serology; Schistosoma serology; Stool ova + parasite; Filarial serology.

questions.question: Q54 (2015). Man from India with groin swelling, leg swelling.

parts.text: A) What is the pathogen?
B) What is the mechanism of scrotal swelling?
C) List 3 investigations that would give you the diagnosis?
D) He presents with left leg swelling, erythema, and pain 2 years later. What is the likely diagnosis?
E) What is the most likely organism?
F) What are 3 interventions to decrease the risk of recurrence of this complication?

cohort_answer.text: A) Wuchereria bancrofti; Brugia malayi; Brugia timori. B) Adult worms live in afferent lymphatics of lower extremities and male genitalia causing inflammation and obstruction to lymphatic flow. C) Filarial serology for IgG1 and IgG4; nocturnal blood smear (10pm-2am); scrotal US for filarial dance sign (Lombarda sign). D) Leg cellulitis. E) Group A Strep or S. aureus. F) Wound care; compression stockings; treat tinea; penicillin ppx if recurrent; for lymphedema - physio, postural drainage, compression.

questions.question: Identify the parasite in the following scenarios: Patient from Taiwan with recurrent cholangitis and cholangiocarcinoma; Patient from Tanzania with portal hypertension; Patient from Zimbabwe with bladder fibrosis; Patient from Ethiopia with progressive keratitis and vision loss.

parts.text: Taiwan, recurrent cholangitis/cholangiocarcinoma
Tanzania, portal hypertension
Zimbabwe, bladder fibrosis
Ethiopia, progressive keratitis and vision loss

cohort_answer.text: Taiwan: Clonorchis sinensis. Tanzania: Schistosoma mansoni. Zimbabwe: Schistosoma haematobium. Ethiopia: Onchocerca volvulus.

questions.question: For each of the following, list if you would use steroids as adjunctive therapy (yes or no): TB meningitis; Neurocysticercosis with viable intraparenchymal cyst; Cerebral malaria; Acute schistosomiasis; Large echinococcal cyst with risk of rupture during PAIR.

parts.text: Indicate yes/no for steroid use in each scenario and rationale

cohort_answer.text: Katayama fever (acute schisto) - yes (5 days pred 40mg followed by praziquantel per Mandell's). Neurocysticercosis intraventricular lesions not calcified and no hydrocephalus - yes (dexamethasone 6-8mg/day divided TID for 28 days, then slow taper over 2-8 weeks; not indicated in calcified cysts with isolated perilesional edema; steroids lower praziquantel levels and increase albendazole levels, partial reason for albendazole use in limited CNS disease). TB meningitis - yes (non-HIV TB pericarditis can also use steroids, not for pleural; if HIV+ insufficient evidence). Ruptured echinococcus - no (not addressed in guidelines or UpToDate). Cerebral malaria - no

parts.text: What is the most common cause of lymphatic filariasis worldwide (genus and species)
57yo man presents with dry cough, fevers, wheeze. Serum IgE is elevated. What is the clinical syndrome?
What is one microbiologic test that can confirm this diagnosis?
Name 2 chronic complications of this infection

cohort_answer.text: Most common cause: Wuchereria bancrofti (90% of cases). Clinical syndrome: Tropical pulmonary eosinophilia. Confirmatory test: Blood smear evening for microfilariae; Serology (DEC is treatment x1 dose). Chronic complications: Lymphedema; Hydrocele; Chyluria

questions.question: Identify the parasite in the following scenarios: Patient from Ethiopia with progressive keratitis and vision loss.

parts.text: Identify the parasite: Patient from Ethiopia with progressive keratitis and vision loss.

cohort_answer.text: Onchocerca volvulus. Tissue nematode. Typically found in Central Africa, also Western/Eastern Africa, near rivers where Simulium Black Fly is present (bites typically during the day). Can progress from subcutaneous tissue to lymph nodes and cornea, causing keratitis and blindness. Treatment: Ivermectin (contraindicated in Loa loa co-infection as can cause fatal encephalitis; if so, use Doxycycline + Albendazole then possibly DEC).
